rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec quarter-point hike ~96%, Jan ~62% (CME FedWatch via Hercules); BoC Dec ~80% from ~65% (Reuters); BoE Dec ~82%; ECB Dec ~90%; BoJ Dec ~84%
rows.read: A December Fed hike is fully priced, so strong US data no longer adds much to the dollar. The Bank of Canada moved closer to a December hike after Governor Tiff Macklem's speech, which lifted the loonie. Bank of England policymakers keep backing another hike, which supports the pound.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US Conference Board confidence 103.3 (fcst 92.1, Oct 91.9); Germany Ifo 90.6 (fcst 90.6); US FHFA house prices 0.0% m/m (fcst +0.2%); Richmond Fed +3 (fcst −3)
rows.read: US consumers turned much more upbeat about jobs, a sign the economy is holding up under higher rates. Germany's business mood kept improving. Neither moved currencies much, because markets were watching stocks and yields.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Australia CPI Oct due Tue 6:30 PM CT (fcst 4.7% y/y); US core PCE Oct due Wed 7:30 AM CT (fcst +0.3% m/m, 3.2% y/y); Tokyo core CPI Nov due Thu 5:30 PM CT (fcst 2.9%)
rows.read: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Australian inflation on Tuesday evening and US core inflation on Wednesday are the week's big tests.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: USD/CHF ~0.8354 (−0.90%); US 10-year ~4.89%, lowest since Nov 10; DXY ~103.85 (−0.34%) (Hercules, early afternoon)
rows.read: Monday's rally in technology shares faded, and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz kept some caution alive. That brought money back into the franc and pulled the dollar down. Possible new US tariffs on 16 trading partners are a fresh worry for stocks.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: Hedge funds (CFTC, Nov 17): USD index −1.3K (flipped short), EUR −76.6K, GBP +28.8K, JPY −23.8K, CHF −19.8K, CAD −72.1K, AUD +38.0K, NZD −23.6K; asset managers GBP −104.6K, AUD −182.7K, EUR +147.2K
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: USTR Section 301 findings expected as soon as Nov 24, 16 partners, final rates not set (Reuters); US 10-year ~4.89% (Hercules); France debt 119% of GDP (ECB)
rows.read: Reports say the US may soon add new tariffs on 16 trading partners, including China, the European Union and Japan, which could weigh on those economies and on US growth. Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs high. France's debts remain a weight on the euro.
